claims.text: The target material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework combines machine learning, DFT, CALPHAD, and optimization of local defect configurations.
The framework can accurately predict conductivity across both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The integrated framework will outperform conventional analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
The oxygen-containing specimen exhibits defect structures and local atomic relaxations.
The 0–200 K interval is an ionization/activation regime, whereas 300–1200 K is an intrinsic-conduction regime.
The framework explicitly incorporates oxygen-induced defects and their associated local atomic relaxations.
Oxygen-induced defect states and local relaxations modify the near-Fermi-level electronic structure and carrier scattering rates.
Modeling local relaxations and defect configurations provides a more accurate treatment of defects than analytical approaches that omit such local structure.
The relevant carrier-scattering and conduction mechanisms vary with temperature.
Perfect-crystal analytical models typically underestimate or misrepresent the conductivity of the oxygen-containing alloy.
The proposed predictions will agree with measured conductivity within ±10% throughout both target temperature regimes.
Conventional analytical predictions can deviate from measurements by as much as ±25%.
The framework is expected to be reliable specifically in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K intervals.
Accuracy is less certain between 200 K and 300 K because conduction mechanisms transition there.
Accuracy is less certain for oxygen concentrations significantly different from 1 wt.%.
Further calibration with experimental data is needed because defect interactions are complex and materials-science datasets can be limited.

The conductivity benchmark consists of four-probe measurements on a synthesized bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen with 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, compared against both the proposed framework and traditional analytical models.
A conductivity error greater than ±15% in either target temperature regime falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to reduce error relative to the analytical baseline by more than 10% also falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires agreement within ±10%, but the absolute-error falsification threshold is only triggered above ±15%. Results between 10% and 15% can therefore fail the stated prediction without falsifying it, unless the separate relative-improvement condition happens to apply.
